FULL VIEW
OUTLINE VIEW
Pretest
Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Describe the differences between neuromuscular scoliosis and other types of scoliosis.
Complete an appropriate workup and evaluation of patients with neuromuscular scoliosis.
Assess the natural history of various types of neuromuscular scoliosis.
Compare nonsurgical and surgical treatment options for patients with neuromuscular
scoliosis.
Outline complications commonly observed in patients who undergo spinal fusion for the
management of neuromuscular scoliosis.
Establish anticipated outcomes, including caregiver-reported outcomes, after spinal fusion.
Background
Neuromuscular scoliosis is caused by various diagnoses that affect neurologic function

Diagnoses include
Cerebral palsy
Spinal muscular atrophy
Myelomeningocele
Muscular dystrophy (ie, Duchenne muscular dystrophy)
Spinal cord injury

Background
Neuromuscular scoliosis is a rotatory multiplanar spinal deformity observed in patients
with various conditions that affect neurologic function to some extent. Common
neuromuscular conditions associated with scoliosis include upper motor neuron
diseases, such as cerebral palsy; lower motor neuron diseases, such as spinal muscular
atrophy; mixed motor neuron diseases, such as myelomeningocele, with upper and
lower motor neuron involvement; muscular dystrophies, such as Duchenne muscular
dystrophy; and spinal cord injury. The association between various underlying etiologies
and scoliosis often depends on the extent or severity of the specific condition, especially
in those with muscular imbalances related to spasticity.
Neuromuscular scoliosis differs from idiopathic scoliosis in multiple respects:
More likely to progress after maturity1-5
More likely to result in marked spinal imbalance related to pelvic obliquity
More likely to be associated with long, sweeping curves
Less likely to respond to nonsurgical management and, therefore, more likely to
require spinal fusion
As an example, scoliosis is more likely to occur in patients with spastic tetraplegia than
patients with hemiplegia. Hägglund et al6 found that, although 8% of children younger
than 5 years with Gross Motor Function Classification System level V cerebral palsy have
scoliosis, 75% of individuals aged 20 years with Gross Motor Function Classification
System level V cerebral palsy have a curve greater than 40°, indicating that scoliosis will
likely occur in patients with severe cerebral palsy involvement. Major spinal deformity is

more likely in patients with thoracic-level myelomeningocele than in patients with sacral-
level lesions; similarly, major spinal deformity is more likely in patients with cervical or
high thoracic spinal cord injury than in patients with lumbar injuries.6
Evaluation
A detailed assessment should include:
Birth history
Developmental history
Ambulatory/mobility status
Neurologic/seizure history
Pulmonary assessment
Gastrointestinal history
Urologic history
Cardiac history
History and status of durable medical equipment use (eg, wheelchair, gait aids)
Physical examination
Overall weight and nutritional status
Skin assessment/pressure sores
Upper extremity mobility/contractures
Spine
Curve stiffness
Pelvic obliquity
Soft-tissue coverage
Previous surgical scars
Pelvic and hip examinations for contractures
Neurologic function, including level of motor adn sensory function of upper and lower
extremities
Gait analysis, sitting balance, and head control
Radiographic analysis
Standard radiography of the thoracolumbar spine
SEND FEEDBACK

3/27

Upright PA and lateral radiographs
Supine AP and lateral radiographs
Bending or supine traction radiographs
Cervical spine radiographs can help determine if instability is present.
Pelvic radiographs can help determine the adequacy of instrumentation to the pelvis.
CT illuminates anatomy in patients with myelomeningocele or severe curves.
MRI is performed if intraspinal pathology is expected.Typically, MRI is not indicated in
patients with cerebral palsy, spinal muscular atrophy, or other neuromuscular syndromes
not usually associated with intraspinal pathology.

Evaluation
To minimize the risk of complications in this patient population, a careful patient history
is imperative. A developmental history, including developmental milestones, may help
evaluate the trajectory of cognitive and motor improvements over time. Ambulatory and
mobility status and changes potentially related to the deformity may determine the
location at which a fusion construct should end. For example, fusion to the pelvis is rare
in an ambulatory child with neuromuscular scoliosis but common in nonambulatory
patients. The neurologic history should include an evaluation of seizure management,
including medications, the presence of Chiari malformations or spinal tethering,
particularly in patients with myelomeningocele, and the use of a baclofen pump. The
pulmonary assessment should focus on medications; the need for home ventilatory
support, including positive pressure (eg, biphasic positive airway pressure) needs; timing
of recent pulmonary-related hospitalizations; and changes in secretions (volume or
nature). The gastrointestinal history should address feeding and bowel regimens, the
presence of a gastrostomy or gastrojejunostomy tube, and the need for revisions.
Placement of a gastrojejunostomy tube may be indicated if postsurgical superior
mesenteric artery syndrome is a concern.7 In patients with neurologic injury or spinal
dysraphisms, the urologic history should include the need for catheterization and
bladder programs. Cardiac history is important because many patients with muscular
dystrophy and various syndromes (eg, Down syndrome, DiGeorge syndrome) may
require cardiac anesthesia. In addition, cardiac clearance should be obtained in patients
with muscular dystrophy before any spinal procedure; typically, an electrocardiogram
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:53 PM
AAOS | Neuromuscular Scoliosis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000037
4/27

and echocardiogram is required.8 A history and current status of durable medical
equipment use, including wheelchairs and gait aids, is important. Querying the caregiver
about seating within a chair and the patient’s ability to maintain an upright position with
custom seat adjustments may reveal challenges in activities of daily living. Patients
undergoing spinal surgery should maintain a relationship with a seating and mobility
specialist to address postoperative changes in body alignment.
The physical examination always begins with a general assessment of the patient’s body
habitus. Substantial cachexia often is observed in patients with spastic tetraplegia,
whereas many children with Duchenne muscular dystrophy and myelomeningocele may
be overweight but have relatively poor nutrition because of a sedentary lifestyle. Obesity
does not imply a healthy nutritional status.
Upper extremity mobility and contractures should be assessed. In many children with
spastic tetraplegia and conditions such as Rett syndrome or arthrogryposis, contractures
in the upper extremity may complicate wheelchair positioning and intraoperative
positioning on a spinal table. In rare situations, an upper extremity specialist may assist
with proper positioning of the arms.
Careful examination of the spine includes assessment of curve stiffness, pressure sores,
the extent of pelvic obliquity, soft tissue available for coverage of spinal implants, and
scars from previous spinal surgery (eg, baclofen pumps).
Pelvic and hip examinations are critical and often overlooked. Hip flexion contractures
are extremely common in wheelchair ambulators. Hyperextension of the hip joint in
these patients results in relative hyperlordosis of the lumbar spine, which may affect
seating after spinal surgery. In rare situations, hip flexion contractures may need to be
addressed preoperatively. Neurologically dislocated hips should be considered because
they may affect wheelchair positioning and the surgeon’s ability to correct pelvic
obliquity intraoperatively. Lower extremity alignment and contractures also may affect
positioning and should be accounted for preoperatively to avoid major intraoperative
struggles.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:53 PM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000037
5/27

Careful assessment of neurologic function, motor and sensory, is critical in patients
undergoing spinal fusion. Because neuromonitoring may be abnormal intraoperatively,
knowledge of the patient’s preoperative function is critical in assessing whether
neurologic changes have occurred. Often, postoperative neurologic changes are difficult
to determine in patients with severe cerebral palsy who do not seem to be moving their
toes if the clinician has not documented whether this is a change from the patient’s
preoperative status.
The relative benefits of supine versus upright radiographs in patients with scoliosis is a
subject of debate. Supine radiographs often represent the true magnitude of a child’s
curve and may guide caregivers, surgeons, and orthotists in determining whether
seating adjustments may be accommodative. Upright radiographs also may explain
challenges with wheelchair adjustments; however, they often exaggerate scoliosis
severity in patients with relative hypotonia.
Lateral radiographs are critical because of the association between lumbar hyperlordosis
and thoracic hyperkyphosis. Other common sagittal plane deformities include thoracic
hypokyphosis in some patients with transverse myelitis and spondylolisthesis, which is
present in 4% to 21% of patients with spastic diplegia.9 Traction, bolster, or push-prone
radiographs may be invaluable in patients who are surgical candidates to determine
curve flexibility; the need for adjuncts, such as traction or osteotomies; and fusion levels.
If spinal instrumentation to the pelvis is considered, dedicated pelvic radiographs may
help address concerns about pelvic morphology based on spinal radiographs.
Flexion/extension lateral radiographs of the cervical spine are indicated in patients with
Down syndrome who are undergoing posterior spinal fusion.
Advanced imaging studies may be necessary for preoperative planning in patients with
neuromuscular scoliosis. CT often is indicated in patients with myelomeningocele to
depict local anatomy and dysraphism but is rarely necessary in patients with cerebral
palsy or spinal syndromes. MRI is routinely used if intraspinal pathology is expected (eg,
myelomeningocele with Chiari type II malformations and spinal tethering). MRI also is
indicated in patients with neurofibromatosis, Larsen syndrome, mucopolysaccharidosis,
and other syndromes. MRI should not be ordered routinely in patients with cerebral
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:53 PM
AAOS | Neuromuscular Scoliosis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000037
6/27

palsy unless a change in neurologic examination findings (eg, a change in bowel or
bladder function) or rapid, unexpected curve progression is noted.
Management
Medical management
Steroid administration for the management of Duchenne muscular dystrophy decreases the
incidence of scoliosis and improves survival
Intrathecal nusinersen or oral risdiplam may improve motor function in patients with spinal
muscular atrophy.
Durable medical equipment and orthotic management may be used to delay curve
progression but usually are not definitive treatment options.
Surgical management
Growing constructs can be used to delay definitive surgical treatment in young children with
substantial growth remaining. Such instrumentation may be left in placein select patients at
the cessation of growth (ie spinal muscular atrophy).10
Spinal fusion is the preferred treatment option.
Fusion to the pelvis should be reserved for nonambulatory patients with major pelvic
obliquity that cannot be managed with wheelchair modification.
Spinal fusion usually occurs before the management of dislocated hips.
Indications
Scoliosis greater than 50° to 60°
Curvature that is progressive or causes considerable difficulty with sitting or standing
balance, hygiene difficulties, or appreciable pain and discomfort
Contraindications
Patients who are medically unfit for surgery, as defined by parents, the surgeon, or
medical specialists. This is best determined after a multidisciplinary discussion.
Stable curves with no major effects on seating, pain, or hygiene
Difficult or challenging social situations that may put a patient at risk postoperatively,
such as the inability to secure sufficient home care
Family members who are unwilling to assume the medical and surgical risks associated
with posterior spinal fusion in a more medically fragile patient
Severe osteopenia with kyphosis may be a relative contraindication.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:53 PM
AAOS | Neuromuscular Scoliosis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000037
7/27

Special considerations
Evaluation of the hips for dysplasia is critical in all patients with neuromuscular scoliosis.
Preoperative halo-gravity traction may improve pelvic obliquity.
Intraoperative halo-femoral traction or in situ distraction may improve pelvic obliquity.
Intraoperative neuromonitoring is routine, especially in patients with intact bowel and
bladder control.
Gram-positive and gram-negative coverage should be considered in all patients with
neuromuscular scoliosis to minimize postoperative infections.
To improve wound healing, a plastic surgeon may be consulted for assistance with closure.11
Patient positioning may be especially challenging in this population, and potential difficulties
should be carefully assessed preoperatively.
Surgical management
Soft-tissue management on exposure is critical to prevent wound complications.
Any baclofen pumps must be accounted for and managed or repaired intraoperatively.
Loosening the spine via facetectomies and osteotomies may improve spinal and pelvic
balance.
Fixation of the pelvis usually involves the use of S2-alar-iliac screws or pelvic screws with an
outrigger connector.
Correction of the curvature should be achieved gradually and should be balanced against the
patient’s bone quality.
The ultimate goal of surgical treatment is to improve the patient’s overall spinal balance for
sitting, including any pelvic obliquity.
Closure should be performed carefully, with special attention to fascial closure and coverage
of all bony and implant prominences.
Postoperative management should include close monitoring, especially during the first 24
hours, and early mobilization.
Complications
Complications are more common in individuals with neuromuscular scoliosis than in those
with other types of scoliosis, and the families should be educated about the risk of
complications.
Depending on the underlying etiology, 10-year mortality rates may be as high as 10%.
Pulmonary complications: 30% to 40% in most studies; complications include pneumonia,
aspiration, atelectasis, pleural effusion, and reintubation12
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:53 PM
AAOS | Neuromuscular Scoliosis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000037
8/27

Gastrointestinal complications: Ileus, superior mesenteric artery syndrome, infectious colitis,
gastrostomy tube dysfunction, and pancreatitis13
Wound/infection complications: 5% to 10% in most modern studies; often related to
underlying poor nutrition. Infection may require surgical débridement and hardware
removal/exchange.14 -16
Dermal complications: Pressure sores are common after spinal fusion, especially after pelvic
positioning in an older wheelchair has been altered.
Implant related complications17-20
Screw malpositioning: May be related to correction maneuvers in an osteopenic spine or
frank screw misplacement because of abnormal anatomy
Hardware failure: Typically occurs at the lumbosacral junction; studies suggest that higher-
density constructs in this region often are protective against hardware failure.
Junctional failure: Proximal junctional kyphosis is common after spinal surgery in children
with preexisting kyphosis, especially in those with relative osteopenia and poor head
control. Appropriate rod contouring, preservation of interspinous ligaments, avoidance of
cephalad facets during fusion, and not stopping at the apex of the kyphosis (even fusion
into the cervical spine) may prevent proximal junctional kyphosis.21
Neurologic complications
Tetraplegia may occur after spinal surgery; however, the manifestations may be difficult to
manage clinically.22
Changes in function may be noted with early increasing hypotonia and flaccidity.
The most difficult ramification of a neurologic injury in these children often is bowel and
bladder incontinence.
Outcomes/expectations
The most reliable outcome after spinal fusion in patients with severe cerebral palsy is
improved caregiver satisfaction.
Functional improvements in patients with other types of neuromuscular scoliosis typically
depend on the underlying etiology.
Patients with myelomeningocele do not experience similar improvements in health-related
quality of life. Posterior spinal fusion may decrease functional mobility in certain patients.23, 24
Patients with spinal muscular atrophy and muscular dystrophies show consistent curve
stabilization without decreasing functional mobility.

9/3/26, 4:53 PM
AAOS | Neuromuscular Scoliosis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000037
9/27


Management
Underlying neurologic involvement drives curve progression. Therefore, nonsurgical
treatment options are largely unsuccessful at controlling curves in this patient
population because the neurologic condition is not addressed. Regardless, medical
management is associated with benefits in patients with certain pathologies. In patients
with Duchenne muscular dystrophy, long-term steroid use drastically lowers the
incidence of scoliosis.25, 26 In patients with type II spinal muscular atrophy, intrathecal
administration of an antisense oligonucleotide medication (ie, nusinersen) improves
motor function; however, the effect on spinal deformity has yet to be established.27, 28
Bracing, casting, or wheelchair modifications are relatively low-risk options to potentially
slow curve progression; however, they should not be used as an alternative to definitive
spinal stabilization of larger curves in patients who are healthy enough to undergo
surgical treatment.29, 30
If surgical treatment is being considered, growth-sparing (eg, growing rods) and spinal
fusion techniques are viable options for patients with severe scoliosis; however,
surgeons should aim to minimize the overall surgical burden if possible.31 Recent
studies support arthrodesis in young children (ie, aged 8 years) with severe cerebral
palsy over growth-friendly approaches because of the lower overall surgical burden and
equivalent overall outcomes.32 Neuromuscular scoliosis has been shown to progress
between Smith proximal humeral stags 3 and stage 4, which should be considered in
discussing the timing of management.33 In patients with neurofibromatosis, penciling of
three or more ribs coincided with progression in 87% of curves. If pelvic obliquity is
considerable (>15°) or if wheelchair modifications cannot accommodate a pelvic
deformity, then spinal surgery should include pelvic fixation.34 In patients with cerebral
palsy who have scoliosis and a hip dislocation simultaneously, the scoliosis with pelvic
obliquity should be corrected first.35
Although fusion to the pelvis is a reasonable treatment option for any nonambulatory
patient, ambulatory patients with pelvic obliquity present a challenge. Most children who
are functional ambulators preserve this ability postoperatively; however, weight gain
during adolescence and overall lower extremity motor function may affect this outcome.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:53 PM
AAOS | Neuromuscular Scoliosis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000037
10/27

For example, patients with midlumbar-level myelomeningocele may lose ambulatory
capacity after spinal fusion, in large part because of their underlying motor function
rather than the spinal fusion itself. Fusion to the pelvis also is indicated in patients with
Duchenne muscular dystrophy in whom the apex of the curve is below L1.
Posterior-only spinal fusion is indicated for most children; however, patients with
neurofibromatosis and some patients with myelomeningocele generally are considered
candidates for anterior/posterior fusion because of weakened lamina in
neurofibromatosis, which is related to dural ectasia, and absent posterior elements in
spina bifida. Patients who crawl for mobility (eg, those with lumbar-level
myelomeningocele) often lose this ability postoperatively. Similarly, in children who play
wheelchair basketball or comparable sports, pelvic fixation may limit spinopelvic mobility
and prevent them from continuing with these activities. Although numerous studies
have demonstrated the benefits of spinal fusion for the management of neuromuscular
scoliosis for patients and caregivers, a measured, individualized approach should be
undertaken in all children because the potential morbidity associated with this surgery is
high and some children are not medically healthy enough to undergo such a procedure.
Patients with Duchenne muscular dystrophy undergo fusion before the development of
larger curves (commonly, curves >20°) because of subsequent major cardiopulmonary
insufficiency that occurs over time. Fusion may be performed safely in patients with vital
capacities greater than 35%.
Special considerations in the surgical treatment of patients with neuromuscular scoliosis
include evaluation of the hips for dysplasia because many patients also may be
candidates for pelvic osteotomies; however, iliac fixation may compromise future pelvic
reconstruction procedures. If this is a concern, pelvic screws should have a larger
diameter but should be left shorter in the supraacetabular region.
Adjunctive preoperative halo-gravity traction or intraoperative traction via Gardner-Wells
tongs and femoral traction (skeletal or skin) may improve pelvic obliquity and curve
magnitude.36 To minimize surgical complexity and risk, in situ distraction with the use of
an outrigger also should be considered. For patients who have purposeful motor control

9/3/26, 4:53 PM
AAOS | Neuromuscular Scoliosis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000037
11/27

and volitional bowel/bladder functions, the ability to obtain meaningful neuromonitoring
should be discussed with the family preoperatively.37
Postoperative admission to a surgical floor of the hospital or the intensive care unit
should be determined preoperatively to avoid last-minute challenges during surgery.38,
39 Because of the high risk of infection and pulmonary complications associated with
spinal fusion, plans for appropriate antibiotic agents and early extubation and
mobilization also should be established preoperatively. For patients with a large curve
and a concerning soft-tissue envelope, closure by a plastic surgeon should be considered
to maximize hardware coverage.11
Preoperative evaluation of contractures, including upper and lower extremities, may
reveal potential challenges in patient positioning. A preoperative trial run in the clinic
with the patient lying prone, if possible, is recommended. Careful assessment of all bony
prominences and appropriate padding may minimize pressure sores. Placement of the
patient in a position commensurate with his or her normal function may minimize the
effect of spinal fusion on sitting postoperatively. Allowing for more hip flexion may be
helpful for wheelchair ambulators, whereas hip extension is preferred for household or
community ambulators.
Careful handling of soft tissues is critical given very tight fascia and paraspinous muscles
along the concavity, especially in patients with a thoracolumbar curvature. Placement of
S2-alar-iliac screws with the use of fluoroscopy or navigation may minimize dissection
distally, decreasing the proximity of the scar to the perianal region. In addition, the distal
fascial attachments on the pelvis often are under substantial tension and will retract if
released, making tight fascial closure more challenging. Taking care to avoid lateral
release of distal fascia will aid in wound closure. Placement of an in situ distractor using
rib hooks and a temporary screw in the ilium (iliac bolt) proximal and lateral to a S2-alar-
iliac screw allows for slow, intermittent distraction during dissection (Figure 1).

12/27

Figure 1 Intraoperative photograph of a spine with neuromuscular scoliosis shows in
situ distraction, which is easily achieved by placing an iliac screw at the level of the
posterior superior iliac spine and placing two or three hooks on the thoracic ribs.
Distraction across the concavity may be helpful in correcting thoracolumbar curvatures
and leveling the pelvis in patients with pelvic obliquity. Adequate rod length should
enable lengthening across the concavity by 10 cm or more. (Image courtesy of Nicholas
D. Fletcher, MD, Atlanta, GA.)
All baclofen pump catheters must be accounted for and managed carefully. A repair kit
should be available in case of injury or need for replacement. If the orthopaedic surgeon
is unfamiliar with pump repair, then preoperative consultation with a neurosurgeon
often is helpful.40 Extra attention should be given to sacral dysraphism in patients with
neuromuscular scoliosis and the associated risk of dural injury.
During correction, loosening the spine may decrease stresses on the bone-screw
interface. Wide facetectomies are mandatory in the lumbar spine of patients with a
larger and stiffer neuromuscular curve. Posterior column (Ponte) osteotomies may aid in
axial and sagittal plane correction, especially in patients with a stiffer curve, and may
decrease the amount of stress placed on screws during correction. Lumbar Ponte
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:53 PM
AAOS | Neuromuscular Scoliosis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000037
13/27

osteotomies should be proximal extensions of facetectomies, with complete division of
the pars interarticularis and removal of the ligamentum flavum.
To achieve a stable construct for fusion after correction, solid fixation of the spine is
critical. S2-alar-iliac screws provide excellent pelvic fixation in most patients, and even
small patients can tolerate screws as large as 8 or 9 mm in diameter.41, 42 Fluoroscopic
evaluation (ie, with inlet/outlet views to accommodate pelvic tilt and oblique views to
obtain a teardrop view) or three-dimensional navigation may help ensure proper
placement. Robust lumbosacral fixation may help minimize the risk for hardware failure
and pseudarthrosis. Although S1 screws must be avoided in some patients because of
local anatomy, achieving fixation at L5, S1, and S2 is associated with decreased hardware
failure. Higher-density constructs should be considered in patients with an osteopenic
spine. Augmentation of spinal fixation with the use of cement may minimize screw
pullout in patients with osteogenesis imperfecta or other conditions associated with
severe osteopenia.43 For deformity correction, reduction-type or extended-tab screws
may be helpful in the lumbar spine, especially on the concavity; however, surgeons
should be aware of prominent implants on the convexity of large curves because skin
breakdown may occur. This is a particular concern in children with insensate skin from
myelomeningocele or spinal cord injury.
Correction should account for curve flexibility and aim to achieve spinal alignment in the
sagittal and coronal planes with a focus on pelvic obliquity. Correction should begin with
securing the S2-alar-iliac screw distally because this provides the best fixation in most
patients. A rod is contoured into the desired sagittal plane and seated distally, after
which translation is used to bring the spine to the rod via reduction screws or sequential
reducers. Pre-contoured, patient-specific rods also may be used to minimize the need
for in situ contouring. Cantilever correction of a larger segment of the spine requires
multiple fixation points to avoid screw pullout (Figure 2, Figure 3 and Figure 4).

Distraction across the concavity of the lumbar spine may help correct hyperlordosis in
this region and generally should be the first maneuver performed in a thoracolumbar
curve (Figure 5).

Figure 5 Intraoperative photograph of a spine shows that distraction across the
concavity (via a compressor in this photograph) allows for better translation of the
thoracolumbar spine to the rod by providing additional space for the concavity to move
into. (Image courtesy of Nicholas D. Fletcher, MD, Atlanta, GA.)
Anticipating the need for substantial distraction during rod cutting may minimize the
likelihood of discovering that a rod has been cut too short after correction. Laying an
uncut rod or T-square over the patient’s spine at the end of correction may help
determine the adequacy of the correction and ensure that the head is appropriately
balanced over the pelvis (Figure 6).

Figure 6 Intraoperative photograph of a spine shows the use of a radiographic T-square
at the end of correction to help assess overall spinal balance and ensure the head is well
centered above a level pelvis. (Image courtesy of Nicholas D. Fletcher, MD, Atlanta, GA.)
Closure may be very challenging in this patient population. All layers should be closed
watertight to protect the incision during healing. Careful decortication of the
lumbosacral region may minimize the risk of pseudarthrosis or rod/screw disarticulation.
One tip is to peel down (ie, from dorsal to ventral) the proximal aspect of the posterior
superior iliac spine, which serves as a bridge of bone and can be used as a recipient site
for bone grafting. Closure with the assistance of a plastic surgeon may be considered. If
a plastic surgeon is not consulted, careful dissection of the paraspinous muscles from
their investing fascia allows for multilayer closure with less tension. To ensure that the
midline muscle can be closed, lateral release of the paraspinous muscles along the
concavity often is required (Figure 7, Figure 8, Figure 9 and Figure 10). Covering the
distal aspect of the bandage with a secondary occlusive bandage (ie, antimicrobial incise
drape) may prevent contamination with stool.

Postoperatively, patients should be admitted to a unit with adequate nursing and
physical therapy resources. This may be an intensive care unit or a general surgical floor
of the hospital. Complications may be minimized via rapid mobilization of patients, early
discontinuation of narcotics, early feeds (often as early as the day of surgery, with clear
liquids via gastrostomy tube), and careful pulmonary toilet.38 Parents should contact
wheelchair specialists early to allow for modifications of the wheelchair after what often
is a notable change in patient height and trunk morphology. Although the patient is
recumbent after surgery, careful attention to skin padding may minimize wound
complications.
Several studies suggest improvement in Caregiver Priorities and Child Health Index of
Life with Disabilities scores after posterior spinal fusion in patients with Gross Motor
Function Classification System level IV/level V cerebral palsy. In addition, health-related
quality of life improvements at mid-term follow-up appears to be unrelated toSEND FEEDBACK
